Subject: Ingress TLS patterns & DNS responsibility for private Redwood endpoints

Hi Kimberly / team,

We're preparing our network design for the Redwood Private deployment into our AWS account (us-east-1). A few of the security and platform folks asked for a short recommendation on who should own DNS and TLS termination for the private endpoints, and what the operational model looks like for cert provisioning and rotation. Key constraints:

- All traffic must stay inside our VPC (no public internet egress) except for control-plane callbacks if necessary.
- We are subject to quarterly audits and need clear key custody statements (who holds private keys).
- We may require client auth for API calls (mutual TLS) for the PoC.
- We run behind an internal NLB / private ALB and have strict health-check requirements.

Questions:
1) Which pattern does Redwood recommend for private endpoints (customer-terminate vs Redwood-terminate vs passthrough)?
2) If Redwood terminates TLS, how are certs provisioned/rotated? Do you support ACME DNS challenge for private zones, or do we upload certs?
3) For multi-tenant hostnames (app-a.acme.internal, app-b.acme.internal), do you require SNI mapping or wildcard certs?
4) Any special health-check/liveness probes required by your runtime when behind an internal LB?

Attached: network-diagram-v1.png (shows our VPC layout).

Can you take a quick pass and propose an ownership matrix (customer vs Redwood) we can present to our security/compliance team?

Thanks,

Alex — thanks for the clear summary and diagram, this is a common set of constraints and we can propose three safe, auditable patterns. Below is a concise comparison and an ownership matrix you can take to your auditors. I've attached a short explainer pack and a cert rotation checklist for operational use.

High-level ingestion patterns (tradeoffs):

1) Customer-terminate at edge (ALB/NLB)
   - Where TLS terminates: Customer LB/Edge proxy (private).
   - Key custody: Customer holds private keys (recommended for strict audits).
   - Connection to Redwood: mTLS or private peered-only plaintext over dedicated ENIs; we recommend mTLS when possible.
   - Pros: Customer control of keys and OCSP/CRL checks; simplest for compliance.
   - Cons: Redwood cannot present platform certs (no SNI routing by Redwood side).

2) TLS passthrough to Redwood (SNI passthrough)
   - Where TLS terminates: Redwood's ingress nodes (we keep certs).
   - Key custody: Redwood holds certs for the presented hostnames. Customer can require HSM-backed certs if needed.
   - Connection to Redwood: TLS is end-to-end; no termination at customer LB.
   - Pros: Redwood can serve multiple hostnames, simpler host mapping, platform-level routing.
   - Cons: Requires a TCP-layer LB with SNI passthrough and explicit firewall rules to allow backend TLS.

3) Hybrid (Edge proxy terminates client TLS + mTLS to Redwood)
   - Where TLS terminates: Customer edge terminates client TLS. Customer or Redwood issues client certs to authenticate to Redwood (mutual TLS).
   - Key custody: Customer holds client cert private keys; Redwood holds server cert private keys if Redwood terminates the downstream leg.
   - Pros: Strong mutual auth, clear separation of who holds which keys.
   - Cons: Additional lifecycle work for client cert issuance/rotation.

Ownership matrix (high level):
- DNS zone for acme.internal: Customer-owned. Split-horizon or private hosted zone is standard.
- Public DNS: N/A for private endpoints.
- Certs for hostnames presented to clients: If customer-terminate = customer; if Redwood-terminate = Redwood.
- Cert provisioning: ACME (DNS-01) possible if customer grants access to the private zone; otherwise customer uploads certs to Redwood's secure store.
- Cert rotation: Recommended 30-day automated rotation for platform certs; 90-day for customer-managed keys (customer policy).
- Logging/audit: Redwood can provide certificate audit entries and rotation events to your SIEM via secure syslog / S3 delivery.

Operational notes / requirements:
- Health checks: We need a TCP or HTTP(S) health endpoint. For HTTP(S) checks, preserve Host header to allow virtual-host routing. Typical path: /_redwood/healthz. If you terminate TLS at the edge, point the LB health check at the internal health path and allow ICMP/TCP checks from our health IP ranges.
- SNI: If you want Redwood to host multiple customer hostnames behind a single IP, SNI passthrough is required and we will need the corresponding certs on our side.
- Client certs / mTLS: Redwood supports mTLS with mutual verification against a customer-provided CA bundle. We also support issuing short-lived client certs for your service account via our CA if you prefer Redwood-managed issuance.
- Key storage: For high-security customers we integrate with your KMS/HSM for private key escrow (bring-your-own-key for server certs).

Attachments: redwood-ingress-patterns-20270212.pdf (patterns + diagrams), cert-rotation-checklist.xlsx (operational tasks).

Next steps:
- If your audit team requires we put a short statement in the SOW about key custody, we can draft language.
- Suggest 30-minute tech sync next week to pick a pattern and confirm health-check details. Proposed times: Tue/Wed morning (ET).

Thanks — happy to iterate.

Adding a couple of implementation clarifications from the runtime side — a few quick items we'll want to confirm in the tech sync: 

- SNI mapping: If you choose passthrough to Redwood and want per-subdomain routing, we can do SNI-based routing. That requires your NLB to forward TLS (TCP) directly to our ingress pool and preserve the SNI field. No HTTP proxy in between.

- Wildcard vs SANs: We support both wildcard certs and SAN lists. Wildcards simplify provisioning but make key-scoping broader (auditor concern). SAN lists are slightly more operationally heavy but more precise.

- Health checks: For TCP passthrough, configure the LB health check as TCP to the ingress port. For TLS-terminated-by-customer, we prefer an internal HTTP(liveness) check to /_redwood/healthz over plaintext or mTLS depending on the pattern. Ensure the LB forwards X-Forwarded-For if preserving client IPs is required.

- Client IPs & tracing: If you need end-to-end client IPs for audit logs, make sure the LB inserts X-Forwarded-For and doesn't NAT the source. Otherwise we can instrument the runtime to emit the ingress peer ip when available.

I also attached a quick nginx snippet we use internally for SNI-forwarding / passthrough testing — should help your infra team validate the config quickly.
